hook.text: Most analysts now draft queries with an AI assistant, artificial intelligence that writes code from a plain request. Interviewers know it, and it has changed what they test: less can you write this query, more can you tell whether it's right.

plan.text: Nine questions finish the series. Six get a full answer, with a query to prove it where there is one. The last three are short.

changed-in.text: First, what the loop looks like now.

changed.text: Question one. How has the data analyst interview changed with AI?

changed-core.text: The live SQL screen is still the center of it, and it's usually AI off, so fluency still matters.

changed-around.text: Around it, expect questions on verifying a query, on what you would and wouldn't share with a tool, on the AI features in BI tools, business intelligence tools like Power BI, Tableau and Looker, and deeper follow-ups on take-homes.

changed-ask.text: Ask the recruiter whether AI is allowed in each round. Policies differ, and they change often.

check.text: Question two. An assistant wrote a query, and your manager wants the number today. How do you check it?

check-read.text: Read it as if a new colleague wrote it. State the grain: what one row means. Check row counts across every join. Ten thousand orders that come out as fourteen thousand rows are fanning out.

check-filters.text: Read each filter against the business definition, and look for null traps.

check-trust.text: Then reconcile to a total you trust, follow three raw rows through by hand, and sanity-check the range. A conversion rate over a hundred percent is a bug until proven otherwise.

mistakes.text: Question three. What mistakes do AI generated queries make most often?

mistakes-same.text: The same ones people make, delivered with more confidence. The first is the date boundary.

mistakes-between.text: The assistant filtered January as between the first and the thirty-first. On a timestamp, the thirty-first means midnight at its start, so the rest of that day is gone.

mistakes-totals.text: Its total is four oh five fifty. A half-open range, from the first of January up to but not including the first of February, gives eight forty fifty. The assistant missed more than half the month, and nothing in the query looks wrong.

mistakes-ratios.text: Next, averaging ratios. One day converts five of ten sessions, the next twenty of a thousand. Average the two rates, and you get twenty-six percent. Divide all conversions by all sessions, and it's two point five.

mistakes-rest.text: Then fan-out, the business rules it couldn't know, and invented columns. Those fail loudly. The silent ones are the danger.

hallucinate.text: Question four. What is a hallucinated insight, and how do you keep one out of a report?

hallucinate-what.text: It's a claim the data doesn't support: a trend that isn't there, a number nobody computed, or a cause stated as fact. A language model writes fluent text whether or not the evidence is there.

hallucinate-example.text: Signups fell twelve percent because of the competitor's launch. Your query confirms the twelve percent. The because is a guess.

hallucinate-rule.text: So make it a rule: every number and every claim traces to a query or a cell you can point to. Let the model draft words around numbers you computed, and cut any cause you haven't tested.

privacy.text: Question five. What data should never go into an AI tool?

privacy-never.text: Anything your company hasn't approved for that tool: customer personal data, credentials, confidential financials, and anything under a contract or a regulation, like health or payments.

privacy-instead.text: Most tasks don't need real rows at all. Share the schema and a few made-up ones. One careless paste can be a reportable data breach.

takehome.text: Question six. Walk me through how you used AI on this take-home.

takehome-answer.text: Be specific, and own the result. Say what you used it for, like boilerplate SQL, a regular expression, or chart code. Say what you didn't, like the metric definitions and the conclusions. And say how you checked it.

takehome-hide.text: Hiding it, then failing to explain a line, goes far worse than using it openly.

r-prompt.text: To prompt for SQL, give it what a colleague would need: the dialect, the tables, the grain, the definitions and the task. Then ask for its assumptions, and a second query to check the total.

r-bi.text: AI in BI tools lets anyone ask a question in plain words, but it only answers correctly on top of defined metrics and clean, documented tables. So the analyst's job moves to building and checking those.

r-llm.text: And to sort five thousand survey answers with an LLM, a large language model: fix the categories first, hand-label a hundred or two to measure it, keep the settings the same for every batch, and quote real answers, not its paraphrases.

close.text: That's the whole data analyst track. To practice, the question bank has a hundred and ten more, each with an explanation for every answer.
